reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: Caused by deficiency of the mitochondrial glycine cleavage system, most often from GLDC or AMT variants
Classic neonatal form presents with lethargy, profound hypotonia, hiccups, apnoea, myoclonic jerks and intractable seizures within the first days of life
A characteristic EEG finding is a burst-suppression pattern evolving to hypsarrhythmia
The biochemical hallmark is a raised cerebrospinal fluid to plasma glycine ratio, more discriminating than plasma glycine alone
Crucially it is nonketotic: unlike organic acidaemias there is no ketosis or acidosis to explain the glycine elevation
Distinguish from ketotic hyperglycinaemia, which reflects secondary glycine rise in propionic/methylmalonic/isovaleric acidaemia
Confirm with molecular testing of GLDC/AMT (and rarely GCSH) and, where needed, enzyme assay in liver
Treatment is supportive with glycine reduction using sodium benzoate and NMDA-receptor antagonism (e.g. dextromethorphan); outcome is often poor
reference.pathophysiology: Nonketotic hyperglycinaemia arises from impaired activity of the glycine cleavage system, a mitochondrial multienzyme complex (comprising the P-protein/GLDC, T-protein/AMT, H-protein/GCSH and a lipoamide dehydrogenase) that degrades glycine. Loss of function causes glycine to accumulate in body fluids and especially the central nervous system. Excess glycine acts both as an inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brainstem and spinal cord, causing apnoea and hypotonia, and as a co-agonist at excitatory NMDA glutamate receptors in the forebrain, driving seizures and neuronal injury. The elevated CSF glycine relative to plasma reflects central overproduction/accumulation and is the diagnostic signature. Inheritance is autosomal recessive.
additionalDifferentials: Ketotic hyperglycinaemia from organic acidaemias (propionic, methylmalonic, isovaleric)
Sepsis or meningitis with neonatal encephalopathy
Mitochondrial encephalopathies presenting in the neonate
additionalInvestigations: Paired CSF and plasma glycine to calculate the CSF:plasma ratio
Plasma and urine amino acids and urine organic acids (to exclude ketotic causes)
EEG looking for burst-suppression or hypsarrhythmia
Brain MRI including diffusion imaging and corpus callosum assessment
Molecular analysis of GLDC, AMT and GCSH
Blood gas and ketone/lactate measurement to confirm the nonketotic state
Liver enzyme (glycine cleavage) assay when genetics are inconclusive
redFlags: Central apnoea requiring ventilatory support in the neonate
Intractable seizures and burst-suppression progressing to status
Rapidly deteriorating consciousness with profound hypotonia
Family history of unexplained neonatal deaths
reference.prognosis: The severe neonatal form carries a poor prognosis with high early mortality and profound intellectual disability, intractable epilepsy and spasticity in survivors; attenuated forms have a milder course, and genotype and residual enzyme activity are the main determinants.
pitfalls: Interpreting a raised plasma glycine without a paired CSF sample and missing the diagnostic ratio
Mistaking secondary (ketotic) hyperglycinaemia of an organic acidaemia for true NKH
Blood contamination of CSF invalidating the CSF glycine measurement
Assuming valproate is safe, when it can worsen hyperglycinaemia and should be avoided
Overlooking transient neonatal hyperglycinaemia, which resolves and does not need lifelong therapy
references: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease (OMMBID)
Saudubray, Inborn Metabolic Diseases: Diagnosis and Treatment
management: Lower systemic glycine with sodium benzoate, which conjugates glycine to enable its renal excretion
Blunt NMDA-receptor overstimulation with an antagonist such as dextromethorphan or ketamine to reduce excitotoxic injury and seizures
Control seizures with antiepileptic drugs while avoiding sodium valproate, which further inhibits the glycine cleavage system
Provide supportive care including respiratory support for apnoea and assisted feeding for hypotonia and poor feeding
Monitor development, seizure burden and plasma glycine, coordinated through a metabolic medicine and neurology team
Offer genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive disorder, with carrier testing of relatives and prenatal or preimplantation diagnosis
Discuss palliative and anticipatory care openly, given the poor prognosis of the severe neonatal form
